strengths: Introduces a simple encoderless Riemannian latent-variable model: latent codes are free parameters optimized with Riemannian Adam while a decoder is trained by maximum likelihood, avoiding intractable manifold densities and Monte Carlo normalizers.

The geometry-aware noise regularizer is clearly derived for squared error via a second-order Taylor expansion, yielding Tr(J^T Sigma G^{-1} J), and the ablation on branching diffusion shows a useful optimal noise regime.
Handles a variety of manifolds (Euclidean, sphere, torus, Lorentz/Poincare) via geoopt, with pseudocode and hyperparameters; code/data links and hardware details support reproducibility.

Demonstrates on three diverse domains: synthetic branching diffusion, hmtDNA haplogroups, and cell-cycle scRNA-seq; hyperbolic latents visually recover hierarchical structure where UMAP/Euclidean latents do not.
Honest limitations section discusses memory scaling with dataset size and the test-time latent optimization bias.
Good presentation of baselines and metrics; includes train/test splits for two datasets and multiple random seeds.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: it combines the existing decoder-only DGD framework with off-the-shelf Riemannian Adam and an adaptation of known noise/Tikhonov regularization; no fundamentally new theory or capability is established.

Evaluation is not fair for reconstruction/correlation comparisons: RGD test latents are optimized per test point while S-VAE, ΔVAE, and P-VAE use amortized encoders; the authors acknowledge this biases reconstruction in their favor but still report these comparisons.

Empirical gains are mixed and modest: on cell cycle, test correlations are similar to ΔVAE/S-VAE and Euclidean R3 gives better reconstruction; on hmtDNA, Euclidean R2 has higher Pearson than the hyperbolic models, and only training metrics are reported (Table 3).

The regularization derivation assumes squared-error loss and ignores higher-order exponential-map terms and volume corrections; hmtDNA experiments use binary cross entropy without a corresponding derivation, so the regularizer's theoretical basis is incomplete.

No generative evaluation: despite being a generative decoder, the paper does not evaluate sample quality, likelihoods, or downstream tasks, and no quantitative tree-distortion metrics are provided for hmtDNA.

Scalability claims are not supported: experiments use only 2-3 latent dimensions and simple manifolds; the method stores per-sample latents and is not demonstrated on high-dimensional or million-point datasets.

Presentation/typographical issues: Table 3 is labeled train metrics only; the text says monotonicity as measured by Pearson when Pearson does not measure monotonicity; noise settings for sphere/torus in the cell-cycle experiments are unclear.
No comparison to the most natural baseline, the original Euclidean Deep Generative Decoder, and no ethical discussion of human mitochondrial DNA data provenance/identifiability.

strengths: The encoderless formulation is genuinely simple and leverages existing tooling (geoopt, RiemannianAdam), which lowers the barrier to applying Riemannian latent geometry. Appendix A/S1–S2 make the implementation transparent.

The geometry-aware regularization is given a principled derivation (noise injection with covariance G^{-1}) connected to the classical noise-as-Tikhonov-regularization result, and the ablation on the branching-diffusion task (Figures 3c, S2, S4) shows a plausible optimal-noise regime.
The qualitative Poincaré-disk visualizations (Figures 3b, 5c–d) are striking: hyperbolic latents expose the tree/hierarchical structure that UMAP and Euclidean latents do not.

Reproducibility is comparatively good: code/data links, explicit architectures, optimizer settings, schedules, and hardware are all reported, and the limitations section (memory scaling, amortization) is honest.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The method is essentially the Deep Generative Decoder (Schuster & Krogh, 2023) with Euclidean latents swapped for manifold latents optimized by geoopt's RiemannianAdam. The whole contribution is a few lines of code (Listings S1–S2), and no new statistical machinery or theory is introduced.

The central empirical claim ("substantially improving correlations between latent distances and ground-truth geometry") is not robustly supported. On the cell-cycle task the gains are within overlapping error bars (Sphere 0.60 vs ΔVAE 0.57; Euclidean R3 0.55), and the authors themselves concede that "test results are generally similar across methods."

The hmtDNA section contains a decisive logical problem. Hyperbolic Pearson correlation (0.28) is worse than Euclidean (0.35 rCRS / 0.41 RSRS), yet the authors pivot to Spearman and state they are "mainly interested in monotonicity as measured by Pearson" — monotonicity is Spearman, not Pearson, and Pearson actually favors the Euclidean baseline. This reads as metric cherry-picking to rescue the hyperbolic narrative.

Comparison fairness is questionable. Test-time latents are optimized for the proposed model (acknowledged to bias reconstruction metrics in its favor), yet it still fails to dominate baselines; and baselines were re-tuned under differing setups, so cross-method numbers are not apples-to-apples.

The geometry-aware regularization is only clearly shown to help on hyperbolic manifolds with varying curvature; on constant-curvature compact manifolds (S2, S1×S1) it reduces to isotropic noise and its benefit is unestablished. The reconstruction-vs-geometry tradeoff (e.g., Lorentz σ=1.0 has worse MAE than P-VAE) is acknowledged but not resolved.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only low-dimensional manifolds (R2/R3, S2, torus, H2) and a handful of specialized datasets are studied, with no scaling experiments and no evaluation of the generative/sampling capability implied by the "generative decoder" name.

strengths: Clean and conceptually simple method: discarding the encoder and treating manifold-valued latents as free parameters optimized with a Riemannian optimizer elegantly sidesteps the intractable densities, normalizing constants, and wrapped-normal approximations that plague existing Riemannian VAEs (Eqs. 1–4). The approach is trivially portable to any manifold supported by geoopt, which is a genuine practical advantage.

The geometry-aware noise regularization is theoretically motivated with a Taylor-expansion derivation (Section 3.1) yielding the regularizer Tr(J^T Σ G^{-1} J), and its practical importance is demonstrated empirically (Fig. 3c, S2, S4). The appendix analysis of how curvature reshapes the spatial noise profile versus the global amplitude σ (Section E) is a nice, non-trivial insight.

Three diverse case studies — synthetic branching diffusion, cell-cycle scRNA-seq, and human mtDNA — span different modalities and geometric priors (hyperbolic, spherical, toroidal), and the resulting latent visualizations (Figs. 3b, 5c–d) are interpretable and qualitatively compelling relative to UMAP.

Reproducibility is strong: pseudocode (Listings S1–S2), optimizer hyperparameters, architectures, schedules, hardware, and released code/data are all provided, which is well above average for the venue.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific: the linear memory growth in dataset size, the bias introduced by test-time latent optimization, and the need for controlled synthetic benchmarks for cross-study comparison are all disclosed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The paper explicitly builds on the encoderless Deep Generative Decoder (Schuster and Krogh, 2023) and Riemannian Adam (Bécigneul and Ganea, 2018); the only substantially new ingredient is the geometry-aware noise, which is a fairly direct Riemannian extension of the classical 'training with noise ≈ Tikhonov regularization' result (Bishop, 1995; An, 1996). The core recipe is essentially 'DGD + geoopt', which limits the conceptual advance.

The evaluation fairness is compromised by test-time optimization: latents for the proposed model are re-optimized per test point with the decoder frozen, which the authors themselves concede 'biases test reconstruction metrics in favor of our model when compared to encoder-based models.' This weakens the headline comparisons against S-VAE, ΔVAE, and P-VAE, and no corrected/held-out comparison is provided.

The branching-diffusion comparison (Table 2) hinges almost entirely on the noise scale σ. At σ=0.1 the Lorentz model (Pearson 0.52) is worse than P-VAE (0.68); the claimed superiority only appears at σ≥0.5, where reconstruction MAE/MSE degrade substantially (e.g., 0.68/0.74 at σ=2.0). This is a reconstruction–geometry tradeoff rather than a clean win, and the text's claim that the method 'substantially outperforms' baselines overstates what the numbers support.

Cell-cycle results are modest: the sphere (Pearson 0.58–0.60) only slightly exceeds ΔVAE sphere (0.52–0.57), and torus results show large variance (0.50±0.07), with the authors acknowledging test results are 'generally similar across methods.' The improvement is within noise for several metrics.

There is a conceptual inconsistency in the hmtDNA section: the text states the authors 'are mainly interesting in monotonicity as measured by Pearson,' yet Pearson measures linear, not monotonic, association; Spearman is the monotonicity measure. Moreover, correlations are computed against distance in one-hot data space rather than tree distortion, which the authors admit may understate the hyperbolic advantage, so the reported numbers do not cleanly support the claim that hyperbolic geometry captures the haplogroup tree better.

Despite claiming generality and sketching scalability to higher dimensions, all experiments use very low-dimensional latents (R^2, S^2, S^1×S^1, H^2). No demonstration is given for higher-dimensional or more complex product manifolds, so the 'works across different geometric inductive biases' claim is only supported in the easiest regime.

strengths: Introduces an encoderless Riemannian representation learning framework that avoids brittle manifold density estimation and amortized inference; simple to implement using geoopt and RiemannianAdam.
Provides a geometry-aware noise regularization derived from a second-order Taylor expansion, yielding a metric-weighted Jacobian penalty, and analyzes curvature vs. noise scale in Appendix F.

Evaluates on three diverse datasets (synthetic branching diffusion, cell-cycle scRNA-seq, human mtDNA) and compares against S-VAE, ΔVAE, and P-VAE, showing improved correlation with prescribed geometry and competitive downstream utility in some settings.
Demonstrates favorable training-time scalability at higher latent dimensions compared to VAE baselines, which become slow or numerically brittle (Table 4).
Reproducibility statement includes code, data, configs, and detailed experimental protocols in the appendices.
Includes an honest limitations discussion (linear memory growth, per-sample optimization) and an LLM/ethics statement.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling 'any Riemannian manifold' is not substantiated: experiments only cover Euclidean, sphere, torus, and hyperbolic spaces; no product manifolds, Stiefel, SPD, or heterogeneous combinations are demonstrated despite being explicitly claimed.

The theoretical analysis and implementation of geometric noise appear inconsistent: the derivation assumes epsilon ~ N(0, sigma^2 G^{-1}), but Listing S2 applies egrad2rgrad to Euclidean noise, effectively multiplying by G^{-1} and yielding covariance G^{-2} (or local std sigma(1-c||z||^2)^2/4 for Poincaré), contradicting Appendix F's stated sigma(z)=sigma(1-c||z||^2)/2. This undermines the claimed regularizer Tr(J^T G^{-1} J).

The MAP formulation is unclear for non-compact manifolds: Equation 10 includes log p(z), but the training pseudocode omits it, and the text only says a wrapped normal 'can function' without specifying what was actually used. It is ambiguous whether the hyperbolic experiments use any prior, making the 'MAP' and geometry claims difficult to assess.
The regularization derivation assumes squared-error loss and unbiased decoder estimates; the hmtDNA experiments use binary cross-entropy, so the theoretical justification does not directly apply.

Baselines may be under-tuned or unfairly configured: P-VAE is compared with only one curvature (c=1.2) in Table 2, S-VAE/ΔVAE are adapted to the authors' architecture, and no comparison to a Riemannian DGD or other encoderless manifold method is provided. Cell-cycle test metrics are largely similar across methods, weakening superiority claims.

Evaluation metrics are mixed: improved correlation often comes with worse reconstruction (e.g., Table 2 Lorentz H2 sigma=1.0 has Pearson 0.81 but MAE 0.49/MSE 0.39 vs. P-VAE 0.42/0.30), and the paper does not systematically report or balance all tradeoffs. Hyperparameter selection for sigma/curvature is not specified as validation-based.

No encoder means test-time latents must be optimized per sample, which is computationally expensive for large datasets; the runtime table reports only training epoch time, not inference/test-time optimization cost, limiting the scalability claim.

Presentation issues: Figure 1/Table 1 reference errors, Equation 4 optimizes over x instead of z, and the reference list contains wrong years/names (e.g., Binns 2021 for 2009; 'Krioukov et al. 2023' for 2010). Some experimental details (noise selection, non-compact prior) are missing.

The 'generative' aspect is under-evaluated: only one discrimination test on cell cycle (Table S2), with no generative evaluation on branching diffusion or hmtDNA; non-compact manifold generation is not addressed.
High-dimensional stability claims are based only on runtime, not on representation quality or downstream metrics at high d; no high-dimensional experiments on real data are reported.

strengths: Clean and well-motivated idea: discarding the encoder and learning per-sample latents with a Riemannian optimizer avoids the intractable manifold densities and Monte Carlo normalizing-constant estimates that plague Riemannian VAEs. The framing relative to AE/VAE/DGD (Section 2.1) is clear and the method is simple to implement on top of geoopt.

Reproducibility is handled reasonably: code/configs/data links are provided, training pseudocode (Listings S1-S2), hyperparameters, splits, and hardware are documented in Appendices A, C, and D, and the LLM-use statement is explicit.

The geometric noise regularization is derived carefully (Eqs. 11-16) and the ablation on the noise scale sigma (Fig. 3c, Fig. S2, Fig. S4) plus the curvature/noise decomposition (Appendix F) give some insight into the correlation-vs-reconstruction tradeoff.

The scalability result (Table 4) is a genuinely useful observation: the method scales to 500D latent spaces where DeltaVAE/P-VAE break, and the downstream-utility table on hmtDNA (Table 3) shows the regularized hyperbolic model clearly beats P-VAE and Euclidean latents on region/haplogroup prediction.
Limitations are discussed honestly (per-sample memory growth, need for test-time optimization, low-dimensional scope).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The method is essentially DGD (Schuster & Krogh 2023) with the latent parameterization swapped for a geoopt Riemannian optimizer, and the 'geometry-aware regularization' is a direct Riemannian transcription of the classical noise-as-Tikhonov-regularization result (Bishop 1995; An 1996) via a standard second-order Taylor expansion. No new theory, estimator, or guarantee is provided.

The central empirical claim of 'substantially improving correlations' is not supported on test data. In Table 1 the test correlations of RGD Sphere (0.60) are barely above DeltaVAE sphere (0.57) and S-VAE (0.53), and the authors themselves concede 'test results are generally similar across methods.' For hmtDNA (Table S1), test Pearson is near zero or negative (rCRS H2 sigma=0.1 gives -0.00, and Euclidean R2 has higher test Pearson than the hyperbolic models), so the hyperbolic advantage is not established quantitatively.

The claims that learned representations 'respect the prescribed geometry' and recover hierarchical/tree structure (Figs. 3-4) rest almost entirely on qualitative Poincare-disk pictures. There is no quantitative tree-distortion, hierarchy-recovery, or Gromov-Wasserstein style metric; correlations use one-hot data-space distance as a weak 'proxy for tree distance' (Appendix E).

Hyperparameters (curvature c=5.0, sigma, learning rates) appear tuned per dataset, and the sigma ablation (Fig. 3c) reveals an explicit tradeoff between correlation and reconstruction. The reported 'best' configurations therefore select a point on a tradeoff curve rather than demonstrating a uniformly better method, making comparisons with baselines that optimize reconstruction loss unfair.

The 'generative' aspect is weak and largely abandoned: the authors state 'generative properties are not the focus here,' sample latents from a uniform prior, and the discrimination test (Table S2) shows all methods near 0.58-0.63 accuracy, i.e., none generate convincingly. Calling this a 'generative decoder' overstates what is delivered.

The comparison set is narrow: only VAE-style Riemannian baselines are used. There is no comparison to other encoder-free or manifold-embedding approaches (e.g., hyperbolic embedding methods), and no controlled experiment isolating the effect of the Riemannian optimizer versus the noise regularizer versus the decoder capacity.

Several presentation issues: garbled figure/table references ('Figure 1 lists reconstruction fidelities' should be Table 1), an incomplete Equation 4 ('where' with no content), reference-list corruption (e.g., 'Binns et al. 2021' vs 2009, mislabeled entries), and vague statements such as toroidal variability being due to 'limited expressivity of learning on circles.'

strengths: Introduces a simple, unifying encoderless framework for learning manifold-valued latents by combining MAP estimation with Riemannian optimization, avoiding difficult density approximations and supporting products of heterogeneous manifolds.
The geometry-aware noise regularization is practical and scalable, with ablations on branching diffusion and hmtDNA showing that increasing noise improves correlation with the prescribed geometry.
Demonstrates strong computational scalability: runtime experiments show stable training up to 500D while several VAE baselines and explicit curvature regularization break or become infeasible.

Provides broad empirical validation across three case studies (synthetic branching diffusion, human mtDNA, cell cycle) using correlation metrics, downstream utility, generative discrimination, and informative visualizations.
Reproducibility is generally good: code/data links, architectures, optimizers, splits, hyperparameters, hardware, and an honest limitations section are provided.
Appropriately discusses limitations (linear memory growth, per-sample parameterization) and includes ethics/LLM disclosures.
weaknesses: There is an apparent inconsistency between the geometric-noise derivation and the implementation. Listing S2 samples a standard-normal Euclidean vector and applies egrad2rgrad, which uses the inverse metric once; the resulting tangent-space covariance is proportional to G^{-2}, not G^{-1} as assumed in Eqs. 11-16 and Appendix F. The theoretical analysis of curvature/noise scaling may therefore not describe the actual algorithm.

The paper lacks a control ablation using isotropic tangent-space noise or a simpler Jacobian/weight-decay penalty. It is unclear whether the inverse-metric noise is necessary or whether any perturbation yields the reported geometry-preservation gains.

For non-compact manifolds (e.g., Lorentz H^2), the experiments do not specify a normalizable prior. The MAP objective in Eq. 10 requires a proper prior; uniform is invalid on non-compact spaces. The text mentions wrapped normals as an option but does not detail or implement them, leaving a soundness and reproducibility gap.

The regularization derivation assumes squared-error loss, but the hmtDNA experiments use binary cross-entropy. No derivation or justification is given for applying the same noise scheme to a different likelihood.

Cell-cycle results are mixed: torus S^1 x S^1 underperforms sphere S^2 and Euclidean R^3, and no S^1 latent is tested despite the single cyclic variable. The claim that this is due to limited circle expressivity is not well substantiated.

Quantitative gains are often modest and sometimes within one standard deviation. hmtDNA correlation metrics are weak, and downstream utility improvements are not consistent across all classification tasks.
Test-time per-sample optimization cost and convergence behavior are not reported, despite being a practical bottleneck for deployment. Memory scaling is acknowledged but not benchmarked.

Presentation has several issues: Eq. 4 optimizes over x instead of z, the text says 'Figure 1 lists reconstruction fidelities' when it should be Table 1, the final sentence is incomplete, and several references have formatting/typo problems.
